title: Reimagining Langdell's Legacy: Puncturing the Equilibrium in Law School Pedagogy
author: Rachel Gurvich · L. Danielle Tully · Laura A. Webb · Alexa Z. Chew · Jane E. Cross · Joy Kanwar

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source identifies AI as a modern challenge affecting knowledge but expressly excludes it from substantive analysis. Its arguments for redesigning legal education do not provide enough evidence to determine whether it accepts the cluster’s claims about jagged AI capability, selective deployment, verification or legal-work redesign.
qs: One modern challenge we want to acknowledge is the role of Artificial Intelligence in the production, consumption, and dissemination of knowledge.
That topic is simply too vast to even touch on here.

st.t: Case teaching: Useful method became restrictive default
st.an: The source accepts the case and Socratic methods as potentially useful while rejecting their continued default status. It materially develops the cluster’s reform proposition through an evidence-informed agenda addressing inclusive pedagogy, assessment, faculty training, institutional incentives and shared responsibility rather than merely adding supplementary techniques around unchanged doctrinal teaching.
qs: It’s time law schools finally abandon “willful ignorance of evidence-based strategies for learning.”170 Instead, they must systematically embrace decades of research about how adults learn and, crucially, train law professors to do the same.171       The law schools we envision would reliably value teaching—including teaching innovations—as much as faculty scholarship.

st.t: Human oversight: Accountability is not effective control
st.an: The source does not directly address whether human oversight of AI provides effective control, but it materially extends the cluster’s expertise-development concern by arguing that legal education should cultivate technological competence and ethical formation rather than rely narrowly on doctrinal and traditional case-method teaching.

st.t: Lawyer development: AI renews lifelong competence reform
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core case for integrating doctrine, practical competence and professional responsibility, and materially develops it through a transparent curriculum-review framework, inclusive teaching and assessment, and an expanded public-purpose conception of practice-readiness. It does not substantially address AI-specific verification, lifelong development or who funds apprenticeship.
qs: Similarly, all faculty should take a holistic view of the competencies required for ethical lawyering and commit to incorporating a wide range of skills along with the doctrinal content already covered in their classes.

For law schools to foster these skills, they must create learning environments where students can view themselves as change agents, actors who can create new rules and new systems instead of accepting the world as it is now.

st.t: Legal education: Analysis should lose curricular dominance
st.an: The source accepts that case analysis and Socratic questioning remain valuable but should no longer define professional education by themselves. It materially extends the proposition by linking broader competency formation to inclusion, transparent pedagogy and structural reform of core instruction rather than relying on add-on programmes that burden students and lower-status faculty.

st.t: Case method: Analytical foundations need practical complements
st.an: The source supports retaining Langdell’s professionalizing and analytical contribution as part of legal education while arguing that continued dependence on its doctrinal framework is inadequate for contemporary competence. It also supports complementary reform by highlighting omitted forms of training, institutional persistence and shared responsibility for change rather than advocating a return to apprenticeship or wholesale abandonment of case analysis.
qs: There is much to laud about Langdell’s vision for a system of legal education that would produce competent attorneys.

kp.k: AI is acknowledged but excluded from substantive analysis
kp.d: This 2023 article supplies historical and pedagogical arguments about legal education rather than evidence of AI-driven restructuring. The authors acknowledge artificial intelligence as a modern challenge but explicitly leave it outside their analysis.
qs: One modern challenge we want to acknowledge is the role of Artificial Intelligence in the production, consumption, and dissemination of knowledge. That topic is simply too vast to even touch on here.

kp.k: Reform should emulate Langdell’s innovation, not preserve his methods
kp.d: The authors credit Langdell’s reforms with responding to nineteenth-century institutional deficiencies through changes to admissions, curriculum, faculty hiring, teaching, and assessment. Their central argument is that maintaining those arrangements by default mistakes his legacy: contemporary legal education should reconsider inherited practices against current students’ needs and knowledge about learning, without necessarily abandoning every traditional method.
qs: Instead of doing things as we’ve always done them because we’ve always done them that way, let’s name what we’re doing, for ourselves and for our students, and then ask, independent of tradition or inertia: Should we really be doing this?
The ideas for change already live in our community. And reimagining our law schools doesn’t mean completely abandoning notions that have been at the core of legal education for over a century.

kp.k: Historical teaching methods served a radically different student population
kp.d: The authors argue that demographic change warrants reassessing the default pedagogy, particularly for institutions committed to inclusion. They report that Harvard first admitted female students in 1950, and contrast that history with its 2021 incoming class of 563 students, 54% female and 43% students of color; nationally, the 2021 incoming class was 57.4% female and 34.7% students of color. These figures establish changed student demographics, not a direct causal test of pedagogical effectiveness.
qs: The students for whom Langdell designed his method were radically different from the students sitting in law school classrooms today.
Moreover, nationwide, the incoming class in 2021 was 57.4% female and 34.7% students of color.

kp.k: Case-method dominance narrows legal understanding and student participation
kp.d: Drawing on prior scholarship, the authors argue that unmodified Socratic case teaching can reproduce classroom hierarchies, privilege disputation over justice, and present legal rules as neutral or immutable. They also challenge the assumption that watching another student’s dialogue constitutes active learning. They acknowledge that skillful, inclusive Socratic teaching can improve analytical reasoning and retain a place in legal education.
qs: That is, the method may provide the mistaken impression that the rules are neutral and exist independent of social, historical, and cultural influences.
In short, students may miss the critical point that we can change the rules.
Finally, we know now that vicarious active learning is a myth.

kp.k: Single final examinations assess too few lawyering competencies
kp.d: The authors criticize reliance on a single high-stakes summative examination for limiting feedback and testing a narrow range of doctrinal analysis and issue-spotting skills. They contrast hypothetical, single-subject problems with clients’ multidimensional needs, and cite IAALS, Shultz and Zedeck, and Holloran Center research identifying additional competencies. Their recommendation is to broaden assessment and incorporate formative feedback, not merely change examination content.
qs: In addition to the high-stakes nature of these exams, the format also captures only a narrow set of lawyering skills.
But, of course, client issues are anything but fixed and flat, and the matters they seek assistance on rarely involve only one area of law.
These summative exams also do little or nothing to test the skills identified by researchers as contemporary legal competencies.

kp.k: Curved grading ranks students rather than communicating mastery
kp.d: The authors distinguish norm-referenced grading from Langdell’s own innovations, while arguing that it developed within the merit-sorting system he championed. Citing Tully, they report approximately nine percent of law schools used norm-referenced grading in 1976 and at least seventy-five percent of ABA accredited law schools did in 2022. They argue that relative ranking can undermine learning, self-efficacy, and mental health, while acknowledging that some historically underrepresented students value grades as signals of achievement to employers.
qs: While norm-referenced grading was not a Langdellian innovation, it has arguably grown out of the system he championed.
Norm-referenced grading is problematic because it’s wholly unrelated to the mastery of relevant subject matter or the learning outcomes that each law school must now identify and assess.
Others may count on their grades to serve a signaling function with employers, perhaps even to counteract implicit (or explicit) bias.

kp.k: Institutional hierarchies concentrate reform burdens on lower-status personnel
kp.d: The authors argue that innovations commonly accumulate around rather than replace the traditional curriculum. Legal writing, academic success, clinical and other skills faculty, together with staff, consequently shoulder disproportionate instructional, inclusion, professional identity, and student-support responsibilities despite lower pay or governance power. They characterize this pattern as reinforcing the skills–doctrine divide and institutional devaluation of reform work; pandemic-era pressures further stretched front-line personnel.
qs: To the extent that there have been innovations in legal education since Langdell’s time, they have largely been either marginal or reactive, and the burden of promoting and implementing these changes has often fallen unevenly on members of the law school community.
Marginal changes are, by definition, either incremental or limited to a particular silo within the law school.

Professors on the front lines have been stretched particularly thin in the last few years, as they have confronted teaching amid the destabilizing effects of the coronavirus pandemic, a polarizing political climate, and movements for racial reckoning.

kp.k: Professional formation requires integrated doctrine, practice, and ethical development
kp.d: Citing employer and competency research, the authors identify a mismatch between law schools’ doctrinal emphasis and employers’ demand for communication, collaboration, counseling, and other competencies. They recommend integrating cognitive, practical, and ethical-social development across the curriculum rather than delegating professional formation to isolated courses. They cite the revised ABA accreditation Standard 303’s professional identity requirement as a minimum impetus for change, and propose reducing content coverage where necessary to create space for practice and deeper learning.
qs: The empirical evidence is clear: what law schools are teaching does not encompass the range of competencies that employers want from new law school graduates.
Law schools must provide all three “apprenticeships” in their training: cognitive, practical, and ethical- social.

Similarly, all faculty should take a holistic view of the competencies required for ethical lawyering and commit to incorporating a wide range of skills along with the doctrinal content already covered in their classes.

kp.k: Teaching reform requires institutional incentives and shared faculty responsibility
kp.d: The authors recommend valuing teaching and pedagogical innovation alongside scholarship through compensation, status, training, and mentorship. All faculty should incorporate learning science, explain learning strategies and assessment expectations, and support belonging rather than outsourcing these responsibilities to academic success programs. These are proposed institutional reforms, not findings from a trial of a redesigned law school.
qs: The law schools we envision would reliably value teaching—including teaching innovations—as much as faculty scholarship.
And as part of prioritizing teaching, we should ensure that all faculty—not just some—take responsibility for following research in educational psychology and how adult students learn.
Instead, we must all collaboratively take responsibility for integrating learning strategies with other course content.

kp.k: Employer sorting and rankings constrain educational experimentation
kp.d: The authors argue that presumed hiring expectations of a narrow employer segment reinforce law schools’ attachment to grading and credential sorting. They note that approximately twenty-two percent of 2021 graduates were employed at firms with more than 100 attorneys, cautioning against treating these employers as representative of all student goals. They also identify rankings, bar passage pressures, and faculty workload as constraints on reform. Grading changes require care because grades can both validate students and discourage exploration or help-seeking.
qs: The employers who are most frequently talked about in this context—for example, “BigLaw” firms—are not representative of the full range of experiences our students come to law school to seek out (and for which we should prepare them).
ABA-approved law schools reported that approximately twenty-two percent of 2021 law school graduates were employed at law firms with more than 100 attorneys.
Because grades occupy so much space in law schools, rethinking grading practices must be taken with extreme care.
Especially in today’s environment, where mathematical formulas determine a law school’s rank and therefore ostensibly its prestige, it’s much riskier to break away and set off in a new direction.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The authors make no concrete claim or prediction about AI-driven changes to legal services or legal education.
pts.d: In footnote 140 on page 147, the authors acknowledge AI's role in knowledge production, consumption, and dissemination as a modern challenge, but explicitly exclude that topic from their discussion. Their substantive claims about pedagogy, assessment, and institutional reform are not attributed to AI.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.d: The brief acknowledgment of AI supplies no data, benchmarks, cases, or supporting authority concerning its effects. The article's extensive pedagogical evidence does not establish AI-related claims.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: AI is characterized only as a contemporary challenge in this 2023 article.
pts.d: The authors provide no forecast horizon, adoption conditions, or qualifications concerning AI's effects beyond stating that the topic is outside the article's scope.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: No specific population or market segment is identified as affected by AI.
pts.d: The acknowledgment appears in a discussion of contemporary challenges for legal education, but the authors do not specify AI-related consequences for students, faculty, lawyers, clients, or legal service providers.
